```{r, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
options(width = 750)
library(orthologr)
has_diamond <- nzchar(Sys.which("diamond"))
has_perl <- nzchar(Sys.which("perl"))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  comment = "#>",
  collapse = TRUE,
  error = FALSE,
  tidy = FALSE,
  eval = has_diamond)
```

`orthologs()` and `diamond_rec()` compare two species. `orthogroups()` infers groups of orthologous genes
(orthogroups) for any number of species, with DIAMOND as the only external program:

- `orthogroups()` - the groups, as an object with long, wide and pairwise tables
- `write_orthogroups()` - the same as files in the layout of OrthoFinder
- `dNdS_orthogroups()` - dN, dS and dN/dS for the gene pairs of every group, with a summary per group

__Prerequisite:__ `DIAMOND2` (run `diamond_install()` once, see the
[Install vignette](Install.html#diamond-install)).

## A first example

The package holds the first 20 proteins of four Brassicaceae. The files are given as a named vector (the names
are the species names), as an unnamed vector or as the path of a folder (then the file names without extension
are the species names).

```{r}
files <- c(
  Athaliana = system.file("seqs/example_athal_aa.faa", package = "orthologr"),
  Alyrata   = system.file("seqs/example_alyra_aa.faa", package = "orthologr"),
  Brapa     = system.file("seqs/example_brapa_aa.faa", package = "orthologr"),
  Thalophila = system.file("seqs/example_thalo_aa.faa", package = "orthologr"))

og <- orthogroups(files, seq_type = "protein", comp_cores = 1)
og
```

The result is a list of tables:

```{r}
# one row per gene in a group
head(og$groups, 4)
# one row per group, one column per species (the layout of OrthoFinder's Orthogroups.tsv)
head(og$wide, 3)
# groups with exactly one gene in every species
nrow(og$single_copy)
# every pair of genes of different species in a group, with the statistics of their DIAMOND hit
head(og$pairs[ , c("orthogroup", "query_id", "subject_id", "bit_score", "perc_identity", "rbh", "relation")], 3)
# genes in no group
head(og$unassigned, 3)
```

`summary(og)` returns the numbers per species, the distribution of the group sizes and of the number of
species per group; `as.data.frame(og)` is the long table.

## How the groups are built

### `method = "rbh"` (default): the graph of reciprocal best hits

1. The proteins of all species are written to **one** file and searched against themselves with DIAMOND
   **once** (not one search per pair of species).
2. For every gene and every other species the best hit is chosen with the code `diamond_rec()` uses
   (`best_hit_rule = "bitscore"` by default).
3. Two genes that are each other's best hit are connected (reciprocal best hit, RBH).
4. The connected components of this graph are the groups.

Two properties of a single search are handled so that it gives what separate searches give:

- **E-values depend on the size of the database.** The e-value of every hit is converted to the e-value of a
  search against the subject species alone, and `eval` is applied to that value. Bit scores do not depend on
  the database. The orthologs of two species therefore do not change when a third species is added, and with two
  species the pairs are exactly the pairs of `diamond_rec()`. Measured on human and mouse (41,040 proteins):
  the single search and the two separate searches give the same 16,827 reciprocal best hits, with the same bit
  scores.
- **DIAMOND reports at most `max.target.seqs` hits per query** (default 10,000, over all species). A warning
  counts the queries that reach the limit.

A gene that was duplicated in one species after the speciation has two copies, of which only one can be the
reciprocal best hit; the other copy is unassigned. `inparalogs = TRUE` attaches such a copy to the group of its
sister copy when the two copies are more similar to each other (bit score, both directions) than either is to
any gene of another species. This is a heuristic in the manner of InParanoid, not a gene-tree reconciliation;
see the numbers below.

### `method = "deepclust"`: clusters of DIAMOND DeepClust

For many species or very large protein sets, `method = "deepclust"` clusters all proteins with
`deepclust()` (its run time grows linearly with the number of proteins); every cluster with genes of at least two
species is a group. DeepClust clusters are protein families: they often hold several genes of a species.
`refine = TRUE` splits the clusters with more than one gene of a species by the reciprocal best hits *inside*
the cluster (one further search, of the members of these clusters only). `realign = TRUE` adds the alignment
statistics of every member with the representative of its cluster. Arguments of `deepclust()` (`approx_id`,
`mutual_cover`, ...) can be given.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
og_dc <- orthogroups("proteomes/", method = "deepclust", seq_type = "protein",
                     refine = TRUE, comp_cores = 8)
```

### What to expect

Measured with DIAMOND 2.2.8 and 2 threads; the data are not part of the package.

**Human and mouse against Ensembl Compara** (19,583 and 21,457 genes, one protein per gene; 16,188 one-to-one
and 5,400 one-to-many / many-to-many Compara ortholog pairs between them):

| | ortholog pairs | of them Compara orthologs | Compara one-to-one found | Compara one-to-many / many-to-many found | run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `method = "rbh"` | 16,827 | 97.4% | 97.5% | 11.0% | 2.3 min |
| `method = "rbh", inparalogs = TRUE` | 19,930 | 88.2% | 97.7% | 32.6% | 2.3 min |
| `method = "deepclust"` | 123,438 | 15.6% | 95.9% | 68.4% | 4.1 min |
| `method = "deepclust", refine = TRUE` | 16,487 | 97.2% | 95.5% | 10.4% | 4.5 min |

(Of the 441 pairs of `method = "rbh"` that are no Compara ortholog, 373 involve a human gene for which Compara
lists no mouse ortholog at all, and 68 pair a human gene with another mouse gene than Compara does.) The 16,827
pairs are exactly the reciprocal best hits of two separate searches (`diamond_rec()`). The R process needed 0.6
to 0.7 GB.

**Four yeasts** (*S. cerevisiae*, *C. glabrata*, *K. lactis*, *A. gossypii*; 21,095 proteins) **against
OrthoFinder 3** on the same proteomes:

| | groups | single-copy groups | genes in groups | gene pairs that OrthoFinder also groups | OrthoFinder's pairs found | adjusted Rand index | run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `method = "rbh"` | 4,616 | 3,487 | 81.6% | 99.7% | 70.7% | 0.77 | 17 s |
| `method = "rbh", sensitivity_mode = "sensitive"` | 4,823 | 3,941 | 87.6% | 99.8% | 77.5% | 0.82 | 1.7 min |
| ... and `inparalogs = TRUE` | 4,823 | 3,846 | 89.1% | 98.8% | 80.0% | 0.84 | 1.9 min |
| `method = "deepclust"` | 4,195 | 2,429 | 84.2% | 72.3% | 80.7% | 0.72 | 44 s |
| `method = "deepclust", refine = TRUE` | 4,679 | 3,259 | 79.8% | 99.8% | 66.9% | 0.75 | 46 s |
| OrthoFinder 3.2 (`-og`: MCL orthogroups with at least two species) | 4,591 | 3,324 | 92.7% | | | | 3.7 min |

"Gene pairs" are pairs of genes of different species in the same group. Of OrthoFinder's 3,324 single-copy
orthogroups, 2,901 are found with identical members by `method = "rbh"` and 3,311 with
`sensitivity_mode = "sensitive"`. OrthoFinder's phylogenetic (hierarchical) orthogroups could not be computed in
the test environment (the tree step ran out of memory), so the comparison is with its MCL orthogroups.

Reading these numbers:

- Reciprocal best hits find almost all one-to-one orthologs and few false pairs, but by construction only one
  partner per species; most one-to-many orthologs are missed. `inparalogs = TRUE` finds more of them at the
  price of more pairs that Compara does not list.
- The default sensitivity mode (`"fast"`) is that of `diamond_rec()`. For species as distant as the yeasts
  above, `sensitivity_mode = "sensitive"` (or higher) finds more groups.
- OrthoFinder builds gene trees and reports hierarchical orthogroups; `orthogroups()` does neither. Its groups
  are smaller and it leaves more genes unassigned (species-specific groups are not reported at all).
- DeepClust clusters without `refine = TRUE` are families rather than orthogroups: see the limits below.

### Run time, memory and limits

Fourteen yeast and other fungal proteomes of NCBI RefSeq (4,776 to 6,472 proteins each), the first 2, 4, 8 and 14
of them; DIAMOND 2.2.8 with 2 threads on a shared 2-core machine (CPU seconds are given because the wall-clock
times varied with the load of the machine):

| species | proteins | `"rbh"`: CPU s (wall s) | R memory | groups / single-copy | `"deepclust"`: CPU s (wall s) | groups / single-copy | `"deepclust", refine = TRUE`: CPU s (wall s) | groups / single-copy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 11,234 | 16 (20) | 0.30 GB | 4,165 / 4,165 | | | | |
| 4 | 21,095 | 29 (28) | 0.37 GB | 4,616 / 3,487 | 68 (44) | 4,195 / 2,429 | 76 (46) | 4,679 / 3,259 |
| 8 | 42,187 | 67 (46) | 0.53 GB | 5,555 / 3,315 | 98 (59) | 5,225 / 2,248 | 132 (76) | 5,990 / 2,972 |
| 14 | 76,576 | 150 (135) | 0.78 GB | 6,393 / 1,600 | 249 (145) | 7,336 / 927 | 310 (175) | 8,060 / 1,282 |

With `sensitivity_mode = "sensitive"` the search of the 8 species took 393 CPU seconds instead of 67 and gave
5,470 groups (3,654 single-copy instead of 3,315).

- **`method = "rbh"`** was the faster method at every size measured here, and it is the more accurate one. Its
  time grows somewhat faster than the number of proteins, and all hits below the e-value threshold are held in R
  (0.8 GB at 77,000 proteins in the fast mode; more in the sensitive modes and for large gene families). It was not
  measured beyond 77,000 proteins and 14 species. As a guide: up to about 15 proteomes or a few hundred thousand
  proteins on a workstation.
- **`method = "deepclust"`** does not pay off at these sizes; DIAMOND DeepClust is built for millions of
  proteins, where an all-against-all search is no longer possible. Its clusters are protein families, not
  orthogroups: without `refine = TRUE` only a small part of the gene pairs in a cluster are orthologs (15.6% for
  human and mouse), and the number of single-copy groups is low. With `refine = TRUE` the result is close to that
  of `method = "rbh"`, with fewer groups found (a cluster boundary can separate two orthologs).
- **Groups are connected components.** A single false reciprocal best hit joins two groups, and the more species
  there are, the more often that happens (largest group: 10 genes with 4 species, 101 with 14). There is no
  clustering step (such as MCL) that would cut such links.
- **No gene trees**: no hierarchical orthogroups, no rooted distinction between orthologs and out-paralogs, no
  species tree. If you need these, run OrthoFinder.
- One sequence per gene is assumed (see `retrieve_longest_isoforms()`).

## Files in the layout of OrthoFinder

```{r}
out <- write_orthogroups(og, file.path(tempdir(), "orthogroups_example"))
basename(out)
readLines(out[["orthogroups"]], n = 3)
# the importer of this package for OrthoFinder's single-copy orthogroups reads them
core <- orthofinder2_retrieve_core_orthologs(out[["orthogroups"]], out[["single_copy"]])
nrow(core)
```

`write_orthogroups(og, dir, ortholog_tables = TRUE)` also writes the reciprocal best hits of one species
with every other species in the format of `generate_ortholog_tables_all()`, for
`import_ortholog_tables_all()` and `retrieve_core_orthologs()`.

## dN/dS within orthogroups

`dNdS_orthogroups()` aligns the proteins of every group, threads the codons onto the alignment (PAL2NAL) and
estimates dN, dS and dN/dS for every pair of genes of different species in the group. It needs the coding
sequences: either the orthogroups were computed from them (`seq_type = "cds"`), or `cds_files` names them.

```{r, eval = has_diamond && has_perl}
cds <- c(
  Athaliana = system.file("seqs/ortho_thal_cds.fasta", package = "orthologr"),
  Alyrata   = system.file("seqs/ortho_lyra_cds.fasta", package = "orthologr"))
og2 <- orthogroups(cds, comp_cores = 1)

# three groups, every pair aligned on its own (no alignment program needed)
res <- dNdS_orthogroups(og2, groups = og2$wide$orthogroup[1:3], aa_aln_tool = "pairwise")
res$pairs[ , c("orthogroup", "query_id", "subject_id", "dN", "dS", "dNdS")]
res$summary[ , c("orthogroup", "n_genes", "n_pairs", "n_ok", "dNdS_median")]
```

By default the groups with exactly one gene in every species are computed (`groups = "single_copy"`), with one
multiple alignment per group (`aa_aln_tool = "clustalo"`; also `"mafft"`, `"muscle"`, `"clustalw"`,
`"t_coffee"`). `groups = "all"` takes every group of up to `max_group_size` genes; pairs of genes of the same
species are not computed. A gene, pair or group that cannot be used never ends the run: the tables `pairs`
(column `note`) and `failed` say what happened.

As a guide to the run time: 200 single-copy groups of four yeasts (1,200 gene pairs) took 70 seconds with
`comp_cores = 2` (Clustal Omega, Comeron's method); with `aa_aln_tool = "pairwise"` a pair took 0.45 seconds.
Species as distant as these yeasts are saturated at synonymous sites: only 183 of the 1,200 pairs had a dN/dS
value (`n_na` and `n_saturated` in the summary count the others).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# all species at once, all groups, 4 processes
res <- dNdS_orthogroups(og, cds_files = c(Athaliana = "athal_cds.fa", Alyrata = "alyr_cds.fa",
                                          Brapa = "brapa_cds.fa", Thalophila = "thalo_cds.fa"),
                        groups = "all", dnds_est.method = "Comeron", comp_cores = 4)
```

`engine = "coal"` hands all groups to [COAL](https://github.com/Plumat-COAL/COAL) in one call (R package
`coalr`, as `dNdS_clusters()` does), which is much faster. COAL computes KaKs_Calculator's methods (`"YN"` by
default); Comeron's method needs `engine = "orthologr"`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res <- dNdS_orthogroups(og2, engine = "coal", dnds_est.method = "YN", aa_aln_tool = "clustalo", comp_cores = 4)
```
